Task 3.0: Corrosion and Mechanical Durability Testing (M-1.3.1, M-1.3.2, M-1.3.3, GNG- 1A, GNG-1B) Design of Experiment Matrix The Element 16 team conducted a literature survey of past studies on sulfur corrosion to inform material selection for testing. The studies in the literature on the long duration corrosion behavior of metals and alloys exposed to molten sulfur in our temperature range of interest (150 oC – 300 oC) are sparse. Most of the studies are focused on corrosion behavior of metals and alloys in sulfur vapor at high temperatures [14-18] (700-1200 oC), hydrogen sulfide gas [18-21], and low temperature sulfur environments with interference from hydrolysis [22,23]. Nevertheless, the studies were informative to understand the expected corrosion reaction mechanism with respect to materials and inform the choice of materials to be considered for corrosion testing. In general, the corrosion of metals and metallic alloys in sulfur is characterized by sulfide scale formation, termed as sulfidation. The corrosion of steel at elevated temperatures in molten sulfur has been described by Dravnieks [24] who measured the corrosion rates from both electrical conductance and weight loss measurements of the remaining cross-section of thin strips of steel corroding in molten sulfur for a duration of 200 hours. The results showed that the metal sulfide scales grow according to parabolic kinetics (metal loss ∝ time1/2) consistent with a rate of attack limited by diffusion through an adherent scale. Similar kinetic behavior was observed from studies conducted in sulfur vapor and hydrogen sulfide gas at higher temperatures [14-21]. The sulfidation behavior is akin to oxidation mechanism in that resistance to sulfidation is enhanced when alloyed with chromium [15,16,20,25] (typically greater than 10% by weight).
